name: P. T. Barnum
role: American showman, author and Connecticut legislator (1810–1891)
summary: P. T. Barnum, the circus and museum showman, entered politics late: a Jackson Democrat who became a Republican over secession, he sat in the Connecticut legislature in 1865, voted to end slavery, spoke for Black men's right to vote, and fought the railroad monopolies.

sources.title: Struggles and Triumphs: or, Forty Years' Recollections of P. T. Barnum (1869; later editions to 1889), Project Gutenberg

notes: First audit. His memoir Struggles and Triumphs (Chapter XXXVIII, Chapter XL and the speech of 26 May 1865) and the speech text on the Lost Museum Archive carry his politics; the Art of Money Getting gives maxims on debt, charity and integrity. Answers are his words (a memoir telling of his votes and the law he carried, and the speech itself), since no independent record of his votes was reached; high only where his speech is explicit. The memoir also covers temperance (he was a teetotaler and lectured on it), the Tom Thumb tours and circus business, which settle no statement. Searched in Struggles and Triumphs without a settled answer: death penalty, women's suffrage, tariffs and immigration (no passages), lotteries (Humbugs condemns lottery sharks as fraud, not as policy), alcohol laws. His 1865 speech uses language about Africans that reflects the period while arguing for equal political rights. Most statements are modern and stay null.
